scope.why: The owner has deferred missions 2 through 14. M1 is played tomorrow and its design may change, so authoring the other twenty-nine concepts now would be a hundred items written against a design that has not been tested. Those concepts stay UNASSESSABLE: the gate is lenient for them by design, `UnlockDecision.contentGaps` names them, and no card of theirs mints — which costs nothing today, because the registry declares Codex cards for exactly these three concepts and for no others.
scope.consequenceOfNarrowing: The chapter gate will pass a student who has mastered these three, and the report will say out loud that twenty-nine concepts were not asked. That is the honest state of the chapter tonight, and it is the state the engine was built to survive.

specConformance.asOf: the version in the working tree at authoring time; select.ts already reads `item.probe` and `blueprint.openResponsePerForm`

met.how: Two items a form, three forms.
Exactly six items per concept, so three attempts each draw fresh items and nothing recycles. Eighteen items across the three concepts.
Three open-response items per concept — one per form. See `divergences` for why three rather than two, and for the case this still does not cover.

met.requirement: `probe` distinct within a form; ITEM_PROBES has six stances and the reserve is six items
met.how: Each concept uses each of RECALL, BOUNDARY, ORDERING, CORRECTION, DISCRIMINATION and APPLICATION exactly once. `probesDistinct` is then true for every possible pair the shuffle can draw, rather than true on average.

met.requirement: Provenance per item, never a blanket claim
met.how: Two released TEA items are mapped by reference in released-item-map.json; sixteen are authored and say so. No authored item claims a TEA administration.

met.requirement: No answer key in a descriptor
met.how: Keys live only in answer-key.json, and verify.mjs fails if a key-shaped field appears in an item file. Released keys are not copied at all — they are pointed at in content/staar.
Every authored item carries 1765 or 1763-1765, both of which overlap. verify.mjs re-runs the same year-range parse @pa/curriculum uses.

divergences.topic: The open-response floor is three per concept, not one, and nothing in the package says so.
divergences.spec: `OPEN_RESPONSE_PER_FORM = 1` reads as one prose item per form.
divergences.judgement: Composed with `FRESH_FORM_TARGET = 3` and the quota being drawn fresh-first, it is a floor of THREE open-response items per concept: attempt 1 spends one, and attempts 2 and 3 each need one the student has not seen. A concept with two would hit its third attempt with no fresh prose item. That is worth stating in blueprint.ts next to the constant, because an author reading `= 1` will write one.

divergences.topic: Three open-response items still do not guarantee three guess-resistant fresh forms.
divergences.spec: Phase 1 draws the open-response quota; Phase 2 fills the rest from the whole reserve.
divergences.judgement: Phase 2 can draw a second open-response item, which spends the reserve the next form's quota needs. With three prose items an unlucky shuffle puts two in form 1, and form 3 then recycles one to keep its quota — `guessResistant` stays true and `freshness` drops to PARTIAL_RECYCLE. No composition an author can choose fixes this; a one-line change in Phase 2 would. Suggestion, not a request: once the quota is met, Phase 2 could rank selected-response ahead of open-response. It costs no determinism, since it is another stable partition of an already-shuffled order, exactly like the probe preference above it.

divergences.topic: Both items on a form being open response is possible and would be a hard sitting.
divergences.judgement: With a 3/3 split, roughly a third of shuffles give a form two prose items on the same concept. That is not wrong — it is the strictest version of the same measurement — but it is worth knowing before an eighth grader meets it, and the same Phase 2 preference above would remove it.

divergences.topic: One released item's key rests on a clause M1's module deliberately does not teach.
divergences.spec: Released items are `SME_APPROVED` on arrival, since they are published curriculum rather than our authoring.
divergences.judgement: True of their content and not of their fit. See `STAAR.2018MAY.G8SS.05` in released-item-map.json: it is the strongest released item for postwar revenue and its keyed option is 'To recover the cost of defending the colonies', which is the exact clause Mission-Slate §4.9 records as taught nowhere. It is included because the item discriminates on cost-recovery rather than on defence — it is the only money option of four — but this is the single riskiest inclusion in the pool and the owner should see it before tomorrow.

perConcept.probeToFormatNote: Not a rule the package imposes — the three recognition-shaped stances took the selected-response slots and the three reasoning-shaped stances took the prose slots, which happens to give every form one of each. The one exception is representation, where the released item is a DISCRIMINATION stance in selected-response form and the authored RECALL item takes its place among the three.
perConcept.openResponseRatio: 3 of 6, which is above STAAR's own blueprint of 9 non-multiple-choice items in 40. Deliberate: the capstone is where a card is minted, `OPEN_RESPONSE_PER_FORM` exists because unlimited retries make a guesser eventually right, and prose is the only part of a form that cannot be guessed.

BOS.CONCEPT.STAMP_SCOPE.v1.why: TEA has published no item on the Stamp Act's scope over printed and legal paper. content/staar establishes this directly: of six released 8.4(A) items, none asks it, and the only released source that states the proposition at all is a rubric bullet in the 2023 constructed-response scoring guide — 'All colonists had to pay taxes on documents and paper.' The finding is real and cannot be authored away.

expectedReadiness.note: verify.mjs recomputes all of this with the same arithmetic blueprintReadiness uses, so the table is checked rather than claimed.

cardsThisUnlocks.note: Every Codex card the Boston registry declares hangs off these three concepts, so this eighteen-item pool is the whole of what stands between a student and a PvP-legal Codex today. The ninth card is the one this content pass minted; the registry still lists two for representation and needs the third appended.
